content: Silent thyroiditis, also referred to as subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, is a form of resolving thyroiditis that includes postpartum thyroiditis. It was initially described as a painless variant of subacute thyroiditis due to its similar clinical course. However, it is distinguished from postpartum thyroiditis by its occurrence outside the postpartum period. The exact cause of silent thyroiditis remains unclear, but it is believed to result from an autoimmune mechanism. Patients with silent thyroiditis exhibit higher levels of activated mature T-cells (HLA-DR+ CD3+), activated helper/inducer T-cells (HLA-DR+ CD4+), and activated suppressor and cytotoxic T-cells (HLA-DR+ CD8+) compared to healthy individuals. This suggests that T-cell activation, particularly helper/inducer T-cells, plays a significant role in the disease's pathogenesis. Silent thyroiditis is also associated with the HLA-DR3 and DR5 genes. Histological findings include lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland, absence of Hurthle cells, and lack of germinal centers. The condition may be triggered by the activation of helper and cytotoxic T-cells, genetic predisposition, and autoimmune antibodies. It is a rare disease, with an incidence of up to 23 per 100,000 individuals with hyperthyroidism and a prevalence of approximately 10 per 100,000 individuals with thyrotoxicosis. It most commonly affects individuals aged 30 to 40 years, with a female-to-male ratio of about 4:1. Silent thyroiditis is more prevalent in regions with higher dietary iodine intake. Risk factors for developing silent thyroiditis include lithium use, radiation therapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma, cessation of corticosteroids in Cushing's syndrome (post-adrenalectomy), and certain autoimmune conditions. Routine screening for silent thyroiditis is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. The disease typically presents with symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, progresses to a euthyroid phase, and eventually leads to a hypothyroid phase before resolving completely. Complications may include hypothyroidism. There are no established diagnostic criteria for silent thyroiditis, but decreased radioactive iodine uptake, elevated serum T3 and T4 levels, and histopathological analysis can aid in diagnosis. Histology may reveal inflammatory cell infiltration, lymphoid follicles, and loss of follicular integrity. Fine needle aspiration cytology can help differentiate benign from malignant nodules. Patients often report fatigue and restlessness. A history of other autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), or lymphocytic hypophysitis, may be present. Common symptoms include palpitations, tachycardia, nervousness, and tremors. Physical examination frequently reveals tachycardia and palpitations, and signs of hypothyroidism may appear during the recovery phase. Laboratory findings typically show increased free T3 and T4 levels and decreased thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) during thyrotoxicosis, while hypothyroidism is characterized by decreased free T3 and T4 levels and increased TSH. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are usually elevated. The most common electrocardiogram (EKG) finding in thyrotoxicosis associated with silent thyroiditis is sinus tachycardia. Rarely, myocardial damage, including ST-segment elevation and arrhythmias, may occur. Imaging studies such as X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs are not typically used for diagnosis, although diffusion-weighted MRI may show a low apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Ultrasound findings may include hypoechoic areas, glandular irregularities, and nonhomogeneous echotexture. A 24-hour iodine-123 uptake test often shows decreased uptake. Treatment for silent thyroiditis includes pharmacologic therapies such as beta-blockers to manage thyrotoxicosis symptoms and levothyroxine for hypothyroidism if it follows the hyperthyroid phase. Thyroidectomy is considered only in cases of repeated relapses despite appropriate treatment. There are no established measures for the primary or secondary prevention of silent thyroiditis.
